# Pregnancy & lactation

> *Pregnancy itself changes a woman's physiology, expanding her blood volume, lowering her insulin
> sensitivity and roughly doubling the calcium her gut absorbs. We cover the nutritional requirements and
> the common problems these changes bring (nausea and gestational diabetes), the external factors
> (activity, food safety and screening), nutrition during breastfeeding, and when to refer.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why folic acid has to start before conception, and why energy needs stay modest in
  pregnancy.
- Distinguish physiological haemodilution from true iron deficiency, and counsel oral iron for
  adherence.
- Explain why the calcium requirement barely rises in pregnancy, and why preformed vitamin A carries
  an upper limit.
- Explain how gestational diabetes arises from the normal insulin resistance of pregnancy, and why
  Singapore screens every pregnancy.
- Recognise hyperemesis gravidarum and the thiamine-before-glucose rule, and refer.
- Distinguish milk nutrients held largely steady whatever the mother's status from those that depend
  on her intake, and identify the breastfeeding mother whose baby is at risk.
:::

## Pregnancy & lactation at a glance: internal and external factors {#sec-overview}

As at every life stage, two sets of factors shape a woman's nutrition in pregnancy:

| Factor | What changes at this stage |
|---|---|
| Internal factors (inside the body) | Placental hormones, an expanding blood volume, a normal rise in insulin resistance, and intestinal calcium absorption that roughly doubles |
| External factors (life and environment) | The factors the woman and her clinician can change: what she eats, how she moves, the screening she is offered, and the foods she avoids |

The internal factors explain three facts that would otherwise seem counter-intuitive:

- Calcium needs barely rise, because absorption doubles.
- A mid-pregnancy haemoglobin falls, because plasma outpaces red cells.
- Diabetes can first appear in pregnancy, because the normal insulin resistance of pregnancy can
  exceed what the pancreas can compensate for: this is **gestational diabetes** (GDM).

The interactive figure below shows how the requirements change across the stages, and which ones do not.

## What changes inside: nutritional requirements, nausea and gestational diabetes {#sec-preg-demands}

Nutrition for pregnancy starts before conception, and requirements rise unevenly: folic acid has to be in place early, energy needs rise only modestly, and iron, iodine and a few other nutrients need particular attention. Two common problems belong to this stage as well: nausea in the first trimester, and gestational diabetes, which appears when the pancreas cannot compensate for the normal insulin resistance of pregnancy.

### Preconception nutrition {#sec-preg-preconception}

Much of good antenatal nutrition begins before conception. The neural tube closes by about 28 days after conception,
often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so folic acid has to be started beforehand (the folate
science is in the *Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes* chapter). The usual dose is about
400 µg/day of folic acid; higher-risk women need 4–5 mg/day (those with a previous
neural-tube-defect pregnancy, diabetes, obesity or certain anticonvulsants) [@mrc1991folate;
@czeizel1992folate]. The same window is where weight and blood glucose are best brought into range and
where teratogenic supplements (high-dose vitamin A) are stopped [@johnson2006preconception].

### Energy and gestational weight gain {#sec-preg-energy}

The energy cost of pregnancy is modest and concentrated in the second and third trimesters: roughly nothing extra in the first trimester, about +340 kcal/day in
the second and +450 kcal/day in the third, and measured expenditure often rises even less than that
[@savard2020energy]. That is about one extra snack a day, and the phrase "eating for two" greatly overstates the need.

Weight gain in pregnancy has a target range set by pre-pregnancy BMI: about 12.5–18 kg for women who
are underweight, 11.5–16 kg for normal weight, 7–11.5 kg for overweight and 5–9 kg for obesity
[@iom2009gwg]. The risk is U-shaped: too little gain raises the chance of a small or preterm baby and
too much the chance of a large baby and a caesarean. Yet only about a third of women gain within
range [@goldstein2017gwg]. The ranges rest on Western BMI cut-offs and may fit local women
imperfectly, as Singapore data bear out [@ee2014gwgSG; @he2019gwgSG], so they are best used as a flexible framework.

Lactation needs only a little more energy than the third trimester of pregnancy, because fat gained in pregnancy provides an energy reserve for breastfeeding. Making milk costs about 675 kcal a day; about 170 kcal of that comes from the fat a woman laid down in pregnancy, leaving a *net* extra requirement of roughly 500 kcal/day, with more fluid too [@faoEnergy2004].

### Haemodilution and iron deficiency {#sec-preg-blood}

A mid-pregnancy haemoglobin almost always falls, usually by **haemodilution**: a lower haemoglobin
concentration caused by plasma volume expanding faster than red-cell mass. Plasma volume expands by
nearly half, outpacing the roughly 25% rise in red-cell mass [@aguree2019plasma], so the fall is
usually not anaemia. The response is to use pregnancy-specific cut-offs and to check ferritin (the
iron-store marker that falls before haemoglobin does; see the *Childhood & adolescence* chapter)
before treating.

Haemodilution does not rule out true iron deficiency. Requirements rise for the expanding red-cell mass and the foetus's own stores (the nutrient basics are in the *Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes* chapter), and deficiency is common even in Singapore: about three-quarters of Singaporean women are iron-deficient by the early third trimester [@loy2019ironSG]. WHO recommends 30–60 mg of elemental iron daily, with folic acid [@whoAntenatal2016], and daily oral iron reduces maternal anaemia and iron deficiency, though its effect on low birth weight is less certain [@penarosas2015iron].
The practical problem is adherence, because iron's gut side-effects are a common reason supplementation fails.
Three measures help:

- taking iron with a vitamin-C source, and away from tea, coffee and calcium;
- considering alternate-day dosing, because single doses every other day are absorbed better than
  daily divided doses and cause fewer gut symptoms [@stoffel2017Iron];
- anticipating constipation, since progesterone already slows the gut and iron compounds it, and
  treating constipation with more fibre and fluid as the first line [@rungsiprakarn2015constipation].

### Other key nutrients, and the upper limit for vitamin A {#sec-preg-micronutrients}

Beyond folate and iron, a short list of nutrients needs particular attention:

- Iodine needs rise to about 250 µg/day, for the foetal thyroid hormone that builds the brain; the
  early foetus depends entirely on the mother [@bath2013iodine]. Singapore's salt iodisation is
  voluntary, so iodine status cannot be assumed, and iodised salt is a sensible default
  [@codling2017iodine].
- Calcium needs barely rise, because intestinal calcium absorption roughly doubles in pregnancy,
  meeting the foetal demand without the mother having to eat much more [@kovacs2016mineral].
  Singapore's allowance still rises modestly, from 800 to 1,000 mg/day for adult women who are
  pregnant or breastfeeding [@hpbRDACalcium], so the target is simply an adequate intake.
- Vitamin D supplementation probably lowers the risk of **pre-eclampsia** (a hypertensive disorder of
  pregnancy) and gestational diabetes, but the evidence was recently downgraded, so the advice is
  modest; deficiency is common in Singapore despite the sun [@palacios2024vitD; @sgVitDeficiency].
- **Choline** may support foetal brain development, though the human evidence so far comes from small
  trials [@caudill2018choline], and most pregnant women in US surveys fall short of it
  [@wallace2017choline].
- **Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)**, a marine omega-3 fatty acid, modestly reduces preterm birth
  [@middleton2018omega3].

Vitamin A is the one nutrient here for which the pregnancy advice is an upper limit, because excess harms. High-dose preformed retinol (supplements, liver) is teratogenic, while
the β-carotene in plants is safe [@rothman1995vitA]. The clinician therefore checks that a
multivitamin is not over-dosed in retinol and advises skipping liver.

[]{#sec-preg-problems}

### Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy {#sec-preg-nausea}

Nausea and vomiting affect most pregnancies in the first trimester, when energy needs have not yet
risen. Most cases are distressing but benign. For these, small, frequent, bland meals help, and
ginger and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) are reasonable first-line measures [@acog2018nvp]. Severe,
persistent vomiting is the exception: its warning signs, and the safety rule that goes with them, are in [Recognising
trouble, and when to refer](#sec-preg-refer).

### Gestational diabetes: pathophysiology {#sec-preg-gdm}

Gestational diabetes is a major antenatal nutrition issue in Singapore, and both internal and external factors shape it. The
internal factor is the normal insulin resistance of pregnancy. By the third trimester of every
pregnancy, insulin sensitivity is 50–60% lower (cells respond less to insulin). The fall diverts
glucose to the growing foetus and is driven by a mix of placental and maternal hormones, with no
single hormone responsible [@kampmann2019ir]. GDM appears when the pancreas cannot compensate for
that resistance [@plows2018gdm], and that pancreatic shortfall is why GDM marks a raised risk of
diabetes later in a woman's life.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a woman planning a pregnancy means to start folic acid once her test is positive. Why is that too late?
The neural tube closes by about 28 days after conception, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so folic acid
started after a positive test can come too late. It has to be started before
conception: about 400 µg/day for most women, and 4–5 mg/day for those at higher risk.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a well woman's haemoglobin has fallen between her first antenatal visit and 28 weeks. Why is this usually not anaemia, and what follows?
Plasma volume expands by nearly half while red-cell mass rises by only about 25%, so the haemoglobin
concentration falls by haemodilution. A low number is therefore read against a pregnancy-specific
cut-off, with a ferritin check before iron is given. True iron deficiency is still common in
Singapore, so the ferritin check guards against missing it as well as against needless iron.
:::

## What changes outside: activity, food safety and screening {#sec-preg-outside}

Outside the body, three things shape nutrition in pregnancy and can be changed: how active a woman is, which foods she avoids, and how gestational diabetes is screened for and managed through diet.

### Physical activity and food safety {#sec-preg-lifestyle}

For a woman without obstetric contraindications, about 150 minutes a week of moderate physical activity lowers the risk of gestational
diabetes, pre-eclampsia and caesarean. It also helps keep weight gain in range, and a previously
active woman can generally carry on [@acog2020exercise].

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out & 🍳 healthy kitchen: food safety and fish intake
In pregnancy, skip raw and undercooked items (sashimi, raw oysters, half-boiled
or raw egg, including raw egg stirred into porridge), cold deli meats and unpasteurised dairy (because
of *Listeria*), and limit the big predatory fish (shark, swordfish, marlin, and tuna sashimi) for
mercury. Fish itself should stay in the diet, because low seafood intake is associated with worse child neurodevelopment [@hibbeln2007seafood]: eat 2–3 servings a week of low-mercury fish. Keep
the everyday drinks in mind when counting caffeine: kopi, teh, Milo and bubble tea all count toward a daily
cap of about 200 mg [@efsa2015caffeine], a pragmatic limit, since pregnancy-loss risk appears to rise
steadily with intake [@chen2016caffeine]. Alcohol is best avoided altogether, because no safe amount
in pregnancy is known [@cdcAlcoholPregnancy].
:::

### Gestational diabetes: universal screening and dietary management {#sec-preg-gdm-care}

Singapore screens every pregnancy for GDM, because risk factors predict it poorly in Asian women: the local GUSTO cohort found GDM in roughly one in five pregnancies, and showed that screening only "high-risk" women would have missed about half of cases [@gusto_gdm]. This **universal screening** uses a 75 g **glucose tolerance test** at 24–28 weeks (blood glucose measured fasting and 1 and 2 hours
after a 75 g glucose drink) [@aceGDM2018]. The diagnostic thresholds are an agreed convention: the HAPO study showed that glucose and outcomes rise together on a smooth
continuum, with no natural cut-point [@hapo2008].

:::: {.callout-note}
## Gestational diabetes: the foetal hyperinsulinaemia pathway
The thresholds (fasting ≥5.1, 1-hour ≥10.0, 2-hour ≥8.5 mmol/L) matter less than the pathway:

::: {.flow}
1. Maternal glucose crosses
2. Foetal insulin rises
3. Macrosomia (overgrowth) before birth
4. Delivery cuts the supply
5. Insulin stays high
6. Neonatal hypoglycaemia
:::

Maternal glucose crosses to the foetus and stimulates the foetal pancreas to secrete more insulin.
That insulin drives **macrosomia** (foetal overgrowth) before birth and, once the maternal glucose
supply is cut at delivery, leaves the baby briefly hypoglycaemic. The mother, in turn, carries a
roughly seven-fold future risk of type 2 diabetes [@bellamy2009], so she needs a **postpartum glucose
test at 6–12 weeks**, then a diabetes check every 1–3 years for life [@aceGDM2018]. That link is why GDM is part of Singapore's
*War on Diabetes* [@mohWarOnDiabetes].
::::

First-line management of GDM is lifestyle, with diet at its centre, and medication is added only when
that does not control glucose; managed this way, GDM carries fewer complications such as
pre-eclampsia, macrosomia and shoulder dystocia (the baby's shoulder lodging during birth) [@aceGDM2018]. Diet works best when based on a woman's usual
food: in the local GUSTO cohort, women eating a "seafood-and-noodle" pattern were less likely to have
GDM [@gustoDietGDM], a sign that a healthy pattern can be built from familiar dishes. That supports
familiar swaps: brown rice or wholegrain *bee hoon* for white rice, and water or a Nutri-Grade A/B
drink for a sweetened one. When diet is not enough, care moves to the obstetric and diabetes team
(see [Recognising trouble, and when to refer](#sec-preg-refer)).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: insulin sensitivity falls in every pregnancy. Why do only some women develop gestational diabetes, and what does it predict?
The 50–60% fall in insulin sensitivity by the third trimester is a normal adaptation that diverts
glucose to the foetus. GDM appears only when the pancreas cannot compensate for that resistance. The
same shortfall marks a raised risk of future diabetes: a woman with GDM carries a roughly seven-fold risk of type 2
diabetes, so she needs a postpartum glucose test and lifelong vigilance.
:::

## Lactation: maternal nutrition {#sec-preg-lactation}

After birth, maternal nutrition covers the mother's own extra energy and fluid ([set out above](#sec-preg-energy) with the energy cost of pregnancy) and what her diet does to her milk. Infant feeding itself (latch, weaning, complementary foods, the infant's own vitamin D) belongs with the infant (see the *Infancy & early childhood* chapter).

The milk concentrations of some nutrients are maintained at the mother's own expense,
while those of others fall with her intake [@dgac2020lactation]:

Milk nutrients largely independent of maternal status
: Iron, calcium, folate and zinc. Their levels in milk stay steady even if the mother runs low, so
  the deficit falls on her.

Milk nutrients dependent on maternal intake
: Vitamin B12, iodine, vitamin D and DHA. Their levels in milk fall if the mother is deficient, and
  the baby's intake falls with them. For vitamin D, milk is low even at usual maternal intakes, since only a very high maternal dose, around 6,400 IU a day, raises it enough [@hollis2015vitD]; this is why the infant is supplemented directly, and the dose is in the *Infancy & early childhood* chapter.

The mother whose baby is most at risk is the vegan or strict vegetarian mother. She can look perfectly well while
producing milk critically low in B12, which harms the infant's developing brain [@kuhne1991b12]; what
follows for her care is in [Recognising trouble, and when to refer](#sec-preg-refer).

Three practical points concern what reaches the milk, or what is taken to boost it:

- Alcohol passes into milk, and only time clears it, so "pump and dump" relieves fullness but does not
  remove alcohol; the advice is to feed before a drink, or to wait 2 to 2.5 hours per drink
  [@lactmedAlcohol].
- Caffeine up to about 200–300 mg a day is compatible with breastfeeding, with less for a preterm or
  newborn baby, who clears it slowly [@lactmedCaffeine].
- The "milk-boosting" soups and herbs are **galactagogues** (substances, often foods or herbs, taken
  to raise milk supply), and the evidence that any galactagogue raises supply is weak; frequent,
  effective milk removal is what drives production [@foong2020galactagogue]. The practice can be
  supported warmly without overselling it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a breastfeeding mother low in iron and a vegan mother low in B12 both feel well. Why is only the second baby at risk from the milk?
Iron is a milk nutrient largely independent of maternal status: its level in milk stays steady when
the mother runs low, so her own stores bear the cost. Vitamin B12 depends on maternal intake: its
level in milk falls when the mother is deficient, and B12-poor milk harms the infant's developing
brain. The vegan mother's baby is therefore at risk even though she looks well.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a mother worried about her supply asks which soup or herb will boost her milk. What drives supply, and what follows for the advice?
Frequent, effective milk removal drives production, and the evidence that any galactagogue raises
supply is weak. The advice therefore centres on frequent feeding or expressing. The soup or herb can
be supported warmly as part of her practice, without a promise that it raises supply.
:::

## Recognising trouble, and when to refer {#sec-preg-refer}

Most nutrition care in pregnancy and lactation is counselling based on a woman's usual diet. A few
findings change that plan, either by moving care to the obstetric team, the diabetes team or a
dietitian, or by adding a test; one of them, severe vomiting, carries a safety rule of its own.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do no harm: hyperemesis gravidarum and thiamine before glucose
When vomiting is severe and persistent, with weight loss, dehydration and ketosis, it is
**hyperemesis gravidarum**, and it needs referral, not reassurance. A woman who has been vomiting for
weeks may be thiamine-depleted, and giving glucose or dextrose first can precipitate Wernicke's
encephalopathy (see the *Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes* chapter). **Thiamine goes in before
any glucose** [@rcogHyperemesis69].
:::

Each finding that changes the plan calls for a specific action:

| Finding | Action |
|---|---|
| Severe, persistent vomiting with weight loss, dehydration and ketosis (hyperemesis gravidarum) | Refer; give thiamine before any glucose or dextrose |
| A positive 75 g glucose tolerance test at 24–28 weeks | Diet first; refer to the obstetric and diabetes team when diet is not enough (the specialist team sets insulin and glucose targets) |
| A mid-pregnancy haemoglobin below the pregnancy-specific cut-off | Check ferritin before giving iron |
| Gestational diabetes in this pregnancy | Arrange a postpartum glucose test at 6–12 weeks, then a check every 1–3 years |
| A vegan or strict vegetarian mother who is breastfeeding | Start B12 supplementation and refer to a dietitian |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a woman who has vomited for weeks arrives dehydrated and ketotic. Why does thiamine go in before any glucose?
Thiamine is needed to turn carbohydrate into energy (see the *Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes*
chapter), and weeks of vomiting can leave her depleted of it. A glucose or dextrose load given first
can then precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy, so thiamine goes in before any glucose. Severe,
persistent vomiting with weight loss, dehydration and ketosis is hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs
referral.
:::

## Does a pregnant woman eat for two? {#sec-close}

A pregnant woman does not need to eat for two, and advising her to do so does harm, because excess weight gain carries its own risks. The
energy cost of pregnancy is about one extra snack a day, and only from the second trimester, so what
matters is the quality of her diet. Lactation needs only a little more energy: making milk
costs about 675 kcal a day, but fat laid down in pregnancy covers about 170 kcal of it, leaving a net
extra of about 500 kcal, close to the third-trimester figure.

## The Singapore context {#sec-singapore}

The **confinement month**, the first postpartum month and its prescribed diet, is near-universal in
Singapore. Although it is patterned by community (Chinese *zuo yue zi*, Malay *berpantang* and Indian
practices), it rests on a shared model that classes foods as "heaty" or "cooling", and the diet it
prescribes is a structured dietary pattern with links to maternal mood [@fok2016confinement;
@teo2018confinement].

With a practice this widespread, the clinician's task is respectful negotiation: supporting the large harmless majority of the
practice, and modifying only its risky parts. These are alcohol cooked into rice-wine dishes (it
reaches the milk), a heavy sodium and fat load, and the wholesale avoidance of "cooling" fruit and
vegetables (the very foods that supply vitamin C, fibre and folate). The same respectful approach applies to
the vegetarian mother (whose B12 and iron need planning) and the halal family (for whom the issue is how supplements are sourced).
